common_name: Sierra Linda Autumn Sage (Compact Coral-Red Salvia greggii)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; performs best with lean soil and minimal supplemental irrigation once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Sierra Linda is a compact, bushy Salvia greggii selection bred for a denser, more uniform mounding habit than the straight species, producing vivid coral-red, two-lipped flowers in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost. Its smaller, tidier scale suits foundation plantings, border edges, and mass plantings where a very drought-tolerant, long-blooming Texas native is wanted without the looser, more open growth of older Salvia greggii selections. It draws hummingbirds and native bees throughout its long bloom season; cut back hard to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep production continuous.

common_name: Navajo Bright Red Autumn Sage (Vivid Red Salvia greggii)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Navajo Bright Red is part of the Navajo series of Salvia greggii selections bred for especially saturated, true-red flower color and heavy bloom production, covering the plant in vivid red, two-lipped flowers from spring through hard frost on a compact, rounded, semi-evergreen to deciduous subshrub. Like other Salvia greggii cultivars, it is exceptionally drought- and heat-tolerant once established and a reliable hummingbird and native bee magnet through its long bloom season. Cut back hard to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering, and shear lightly after each flush to keep the plant tidy and blooming continuously.

common_name: Lanai Twister Pink Verbena (Bicolor Pink-and-White Trailing Verbena)

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Lanai Twister Pink is part of the popular Lanai trailing verbena series, producing dense clusters of bicolor flowers with a bright pink outer edge surrounding a white center, giving each flower cluster a distinctive pinwheel, two-toned effect unlike the solid-color verbena cultivars more commonly grown. Its low, spreading, trailing habit fits hanging baskets, window boxes, and the tops of raised beds and retaining walls where it can cascade over the edge, blooming nearly continuously from spring through frost. Shear the plant back by about a third periodically through the season to keep growth dense and encourage continued bloom, and expect it to perform as a warm-season annual outside its hardy zones.

common_name: Meteor Shower Verbena (Vigorous Purple-Blue Trailing Verbena)

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Meteor Shower is notably vigorous and spreads quickly, so give it room or plan to shear back periodically.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, giving the plant plenty of room to spread. Meteor Shower is a vigorous, fast-spreading trailing verbena bred by Proven Winners for exceptional coverage and heavy, dense clusters of rich purple-blue flowers produced almost continuously from spring through frost. Its rapid, wide-spreading growth makes it especially effective as a fast groundcover for sunny slopes, the tops of retaining walls, and large hanging baskets or mixed containers where a bold trailing accent is wanted quickly. It shows good resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures verbena in humid weather; shear back by about a third if growth becomes leggy to refresh density and bloom.

planting.note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Gold Mound is a compact, low-mounding lantana selected for its dense, tidy habit and solid clusters of bright golden-yellow flowers produced almost continuously from late spring through frost, drawing butterflies heavily throughout the season. Its smaller, more restrained scale than tall lantana cultivars like Miss Huff fits foundation plantings, border edges, and mass plantings where a lower, more uniform mound is wanted. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil with ease once established; cut back hard in late winter after the coldest weather passes to remove any winter-damaged growth and encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

common_name: Chapel Hill Yellow Lantana (Cold-Hardy Yellow Native Selection)

planting.note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; more cold-hardy than most lantana cultivars, often returning reliably from the roots after mild winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Chapel Hill Yellow was selected by the North Carolina Botanical Garden for improved cold hardiness compared to typical lantana cultivars, regularly surviving winters as a root-hardy perennial in areas where less hardy selections are killed outright, while producing clusters of clear golden-yellow flowers continuously from late spring through frost. Its vigorous, upright growth and heavy, long-lasting bloom make it a strong butterfly and pollinator plant for a sunny border in regions at the colder edge of lantana's usual perennial range. It tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with ease once established; cut back hard in late winter after the coldest weather passes to remove winter-damaged growth and promote vigorous new flowering.

common_name: Marie Pavie Rose (Fragrant White Polyantha Landscape Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Introduced in 1888, Marie Pavie is a classic polyantha rose producing dense clusters of small, fragrant, blush-white double flowers almost continuously from spring through frost on a compact, nearly thornless, well-branched shrub. It is exceptionally disease-resistant and low-maintenance by antique-rose standards, tolerating heat and humidity well and needing little more than an annual pruning, making it a long-favored, reliable choice for Southern gardens and cottage-style borders where a smaller-scale, old-fashioned rose is wanted. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued bloom, and prune to shape in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Spice China Rose (Fragrant Antique Blush China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Spice is an antique China rose valued for its nearly continuous bloom cycle and strong, spicy-sweet fragrance, producing small, semi-double, soft blush-pink flowers that deepen in color with age and heat, in the classic China rose pattern of near-constant rebloom rather than the flush-and-rest cycle typical of many modern shrub roses. Like other China roses, it is notably heat-tolerant and performs especially well in warm, humid Southern climates where many modern hybrid tea roses struggle, needing only light, infrequent pruning to maintain its naturally graceful, arching form. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the continuous bloom cycle going, and mulch well, since China roses are less cold-hardy than many modern landscape rose cultivars.
